days.title: Account Setup And Not Getting A Surprise Bill

tasks.title: Create an AWS account and complete verification. Use a password manager for the root password.
Before anything else, set a billing alarm at ten dollars. Confirm the alert email arrives.
Create an AWS Budget with a hard monthly limit so you get warned twice, not once.
Read exactly what the free tier covers and which three services most often cause bills.
Turn on MFA for the root account, then write down that you will not use root again.
Pick one region and stick to it all month. Note why resources in other regions get forgotten.

days.title: IAM Users, Groups And The CLI

tasks.title: Create an IAM user for yourself with MFA and stop using root entirely.
Create a group, attach a policy to the group, and put your user in it.
Create access keys for your user and store them somewhere you would not commit to git.
Install the AWS CLI on your VM and configure it with aws configure.
Run aws sts get-caller-identity and read what it tells you about who you are.
Do the same small task twice, once in the console and once in the CLI. Compare them.
Read a policy document and identify Effect, Action, Resource and Condition.
Learn the difference between AWS managed policies, customer managed policies and inline policies.
Write a custom policy that allows reading one S3 bucket and nothing else.
Attach your restrictive policy to a test user and prove it cannot do anything extra.
Use the IAM policy simulator to check a permission before you deploy it.
Break it: remove a permission your CLI needs, read the exact denial message, then restore it.

days.title: IAM Roles And Why They Beat Keys

tasks.title: Learn what an IAM role is and how it differs from a user with access keys.
Read a trust policy and work out which principal is allowed to assume the role.
Create a role that an EC2 instance can assume, with read only S3 access.
Assume a role from the CLI and watch your identity change with get-caller-identity.
Write down why putting access keys on a server is a bad idea and what to use instead.
Check the billing dashboard. Make this the last task of every day from now on.
Create a VPC with the CIDR block 10.0.0.0/16 and nothing else in it yet.
Plan four subnets on paper before creating any: two public, two private, across two zones.
Create the four subnets you planned, each in the correct availability zone.
Learn what an availability zone is and why you spread subnets across two of them.
Look at the default VPC and list three ways yours is different from it.
Leave the VPC in place, but confirm no billable resources exist inside it yet.
Create an internet gateway and attach it to your VPC.
Create a route table with a default route to the internet gateway and associate your public subnets.
Leave the private subnets on a route table with no internet gateway route.
Compare an AWS route table to the ip route output you read on day 32.
Prove which subnets are public and which are private by reading the route tables alone.
Check the billing dashboard before you close the laptop.
Create a security group that allows only SSH from your own home IP address.
Learn what stateful means for a security group and why you rarely write outbound rules.
Look at the default network ACL and learn how it differs from a security group.
Write down how security groups compare to the ufw rules you wrote on day 45.
Create a security group whose rule allows traffic from another security group, not an IP.
Break it: remove your SSH rule while connected, then recover access from the console.
Work out why a private instance still needs outbound internet to install packages.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and note its hourly cost before you do.
Point the private route table at the NAT gateway and confirm the route appears.
Read what a NAT gateway costs per hour and per gigabyte. Write the number in your notes.
Read what a VPC endpoint is and how it can replace NAT traffic for some services.
Delete the NAT gateway at the end of the day. Rebuild it tomorrow if you need it.
Create an EC2 key pair and store the private key with permissions 400.
Launch a t3.micro instance into a public subnet with your SSH security group.
SSH into the instance from your VM and run the Linux commands you learned in Month 1.
Query the instance metadata endpoint and find the instance ID and availability zone.
Read what the letters and numbers in an instance type name mean.
Terminate the instance at the end of the day and confirm it is gone.
Launch an instance with a user data script that installs and starts nginx automatically.
Reach the nginx default page in a browser without ever SSHing into the machine.
Read the cloud init log on the instance to see exactly what your script did.
Break it: put an error in the user data script, launch it, then find the failure in the log.
Rewrite the script so running it twice causes no damage.
Terminate everything and check the billing dashboard.
Learn what an EBS volume is and why it survives an instance stop but not always a terminate.
Attach a second EBS volume to an instance, format it and mount it using day 21 skills.
Take a snapshot of the volume and note that snapshots are stored in S3 behind the scenes.
Create a new volume from the snapshot, attach it to a fresh instance and confirm the data.
Create a custom AMI from a configured instance and launch a new instance from it.
Delete the volumes, snapshots and AMI you created. Snapshots cost money quietly.

days.title: Elastic IPs, DNS Names And Reaching Instances

tasks.title: Learn the difference between an auto assigned public IP and an Elastic IP.
Allocate an Elastic IP, attach it to an instance and confirm it survives a stop and start.
Find out when an unattached Elastic IP starts costing money.
Use the private DNS name to reach one instance from another inside the VPC.
Release the Elastic IP at the end of the day.
Create a bucket and upload files with both the console and the CLI.
Learn why object storage is not a filesystem and what that means in practice.
Use aws s3 sync to push a whole folder and then run it again to see what changes.
Turn on versioning, overwrite a file, and recover the previous version.
Read what the storage classes are and when Glacier makes sense.
Check the billing dashboard.
Look at Block Public Access and understand why it is on by default.
Write a bucket policy that allows read access to one prefix only.
Give an EC2 instance access to the bucket using the role from day 54, not access keys.
Generate a presigned URL and confirm it expires.
Break it: apply a policy that locks you out of your own bucket, then work out how to recover.
Read one real story of a public S3 bucket leak and write down what went wrong.
Host a static site from S3 and reach it over the website endpoint.
Configure the index document and the error document and test a missing page.
Read what CloudFront adds in front of S3 and why HTTPS needs it.
Write down when you would use S3 hosting and when you would use the nginx setup from day 43.
Empty and delete the bucket when you are finished with it.
Create a DB subnet group using your two private subnets.
Launch a small PostgreSQL RDS instance with public access turned off.
Create a security group that only allows port 5432 from your application security group.
Connect to the database from an EC2 instance and run one query.
Prove you cannot reach the database from your laptop, and explain why that is correct.
Stop or delete the RDS instance at the end of the day. It is the most expensive thing here.
Take a manual RDS snapshot and read how long automated backups are kept.
Restore the snapshot into a new instance and confirm the data arrived intact.
Learn what RPO and RTO mean and write down what they would be for your cargo system.
Write a one page backup and recovery plan for a small production database.
Delete the restored instance and any snapshots you no longer need.
Launch two instances behind the same user data script so both serve a page.
Create a target group and register both instances in it.
Create an Application Load Balancer in your public subnets pointing at the target group.
Configure a health check, then stop one instance and watch it leave the pool.
Compare the ALB to the nginx upstream block you wrote on day 49.
Delete the load balancer at the end of the day. It bills by the hour.

days.title: HTTPS With ACM And Private Backends

tasks.title: Request a certificate in ACM and complete the validation step.
Add an HTTPS listener to the load balancer using the certificate.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS at the load balancer and confirm it with curl.
Move the instances into private subnets so only the load balancer can reach them.
Write down how this compares to terminating TLS at nginx on day 49.
Tear down everything you created today and check the bill.
Find CPU and network metrics for an instance and read them over a one hour window.
Install the CloudWatch agent so memory and disk metrics appear, since they are not there by default.
Send the nginx access log from an instance into a CloudWatch log group.
Query your logs with Logs Insights to count requests by status code.
Set a log retention period and explain why forever is an expensive default.
Check the billing dashboard.

days.title: Alarms And Knowing When Things Break

tasks.title: Create an alarm that fires when instance CPU stays above a threshold.
Create an SNS topic, subscribe your email, and confirm the subscription.
Deliberately load the CPU until the alarm fires and the email arrives.
Create a metric filter that alarms when a specific error appears in your logs.
Write down three alarms worth waking up for and three that would just be noise.
Delete the test alarms you no longer want.
Open Cost Explorer and find which service has cost you the most this month.
Tag every resource you create with a project and an owner tag.
Hunt for orphaned resources: unattached volumes, unused Elastic IPs, old snapshots.
Read three ways to cut cost: right sizing, stopping unused instances and removing NAT gateways.
Write a teardown checklist you will run at the end of every AWS day from now on.
Draw the target architecture on paper before you build anything: VPC, ALB, app, database.
Build the VPC, subnets, route tables, internet gateway and NAT for the capstone.
Create three security groups: load balancer, application and database, each referencing the one above.
Launch two application instances in private subnets using a user data script.
Prove the application instances have no public IP and cannot be reached directly.
Launch the database in a private subnet reachable only from the application security group.
Put the load balancer in front with HTTPS and a working health check.
Ship application logs to CloudWatch and create one alarm that fires when the app dies.
Load the site over HTTPS and trace one request from the load balancer log to the app log.
Record what this whole stack costs per day so you know what you are running.

days.title: Break It, Fix It, Tear It Down

tasks.title: Write down the working state of every component before anyone touches it.
Have a friend break one thing without telling you: a security group, a route, or the app itself.
Diagnose it using CloudWatch, the load balancer health checks and your day 38 checklist.
Fix the fault and confirm the site is healthy again from outside the VPC.
Write the incident up: what broke, how you found it, how long it took, what you would automate.
Push the architecture diagram and the write up to your GitHub repo.
Run your teardown checklist. Confirm the bill stops growing before you sleep.

questions.prompt: What should you set up before creating any billable AWS resource?
options: A billing alarm and a budget
questions.explanation: Cost alerts are the only thing standing between a forgotten resource and a large bill.

questions.prompt: Why should you stop using the root account after setup?
options: It has unlimited power and cannot be restricted
questions.explanation: Root can do anything, so daily work should happen under an IAM user with limited permissions.

questions.prompt: What are the four parts of an IAM policy statement?
questions.explanation: Effect decides allow or deny, Action names the API calls, Resource names the targets and Condition adds limits.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of an IAM role over access keys on a server?
options: Credentials are temporary and never stored on the instance
questions.explanation: Roles hand out short lived credentials automatically, so there is no long lived secret to leak.

questions.prompt: Which command tells you which identity your CLI is currently using?
questions.explanation: get-caller-identity reports the account, user ID and ARN behind the current credentials.

questions.prompt: What does a CIDR block of 10.0.0.0/16 give you?
questions.explanation: Sixteen network bits leave sixteen host bits, which is 65536 addresses in total.

questions.prompt: What is an availability zone?
options: An isolated location within a region
questions.explanation: Zones are physically separate locations in one region, which is why you spread subnets across them.

questions.prompt: Why spread subnets across two availability zones?
options: So one zone failing does not take everything down
questions.explanation: Running in more than one zone is the basic protection against a single location failing.

questions.prompt: What makes a subnet public rather than private?
options: A route to an internet gateway in its route table
questions.explanation: The route table decides it, not the subnet itself.

questions.prompt: What does an internet gateway do?
options: Connects a VPC to the internet
questions.explanation: It is the door between your VPC and the public internet.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good reason to pick one region and stay in it?
options: Resources in forgotten regions still cost money
IAM only works in one region
questions.explanation: Resources left running in a region you never look at are a common source of surprise charges.

questions.prompt: What does MFA add to an account?
options: A second factor beyond the password
questions.explanation: Multi factor authentication means a stolen password alone is not enough to get in.

questions.prompt: The free tier means you cannot be charged during your first year.
questions.explanation: Plenty of services sit outside the free tier, and exceeding free tier limits also produces charges.

questions.prompt: An IAM policy with no explicit allow results in access being denied.
questions.explanation: AWS denies by default, so permissions only exist where something explicitly grants them.

questions.prompt: You should plan your subnet CIDR ranges before creating the subnets.
questions.explanation: Changing a subnet range later means rebuilding it, so the planning has to come first.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a security group is stateful?
options: Return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted
questions.explanation: Because it tracks connections, you rarely need to write matching outbound rules.

questions.prompt: What is one key difference between a security group and a network ACL?
options: Network ACLs are stateless and support deny rules
Security groups work at the subnet level
questions.explanation: NACLs evaluate each direction separately and can explicitly deny, which security groups cannot.

questions.prompt: What can a security group rule reference as its source?
options: An IP range or another security group
questions.explanation: Referencing another security group is how you let the app tier talk to the database tier cleanly.

questions.prompt: Why does a private instance need a NAT gateway?
options: To make outbound connections such as package downloads
questions.explanation: NAT lets instances reach out without allowing anyone to reach in.

questions.prompt: What is a common surprise about NAT gateway pricing?
options: It charges per hour and per gigabyte processed
questions.explanation: The hourly charge runs whether you use it or not, and data processing costs stack on top.

questions.prompt: Where must a NAT gateway be placed?
questions.explanation: It needs a route to the internet gateway, so it lives in a public subnet.

questions.prompt: What does EC2 user data do?
options: Runs a script when the instance first boots
questions.explanation: User data lets you configure an instance automatically at launch without connecting to it.

questions.prompt: Where would you look to see whether a user data script succeeded?
options: The cloud init log on the instance
questions.explanation: Cloud init writes a log of exactly what ran and what failed.

questions.prompt: What is the instance metadata endpoint used for?
options: Information about the instance itself, such as its ID and zone
questions.explanation: An instance can query metadata to learn about itself and to fetch role credentials.

questions.prompt: Why should a startup script be safe to run twice?
options: Because reruns should not break or duplicate anything
questions.explanation: Scripts that only work once cause failures the moment an instance is replaced or rebooted.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to give an EC2 instance access to S3?
options: Copy access keys onto the instance
Attach an IAM role to the instance
questions.explanation: The role supplies temporary credentials automatically with nothing stored on disk.

questions.prompt: You removed your own SSH rule from a security group. What is the recovery path?
options: Re-add the rule from the console or CLI
Wait for the rule to expire
questions.explanation: The console does not depend on SSH, so you can restore the rule from there.

questions.prompt: A security group applies to an instance, while a network ACL applies to a subnet.
questions.explanation: The two operate at different levels, which is why they are often used together.

questions.prompt: Deleting a NAT gateway at the end of a practice day is a reasonable way to control cost.
questions.explanation: It is one of the more expensive resources to leave idle, and it is quick to recreate.

questions.prompt: An instance in a private subnet with no NAT can still install packages from the internet.
questions.explanation: Without a route out through NAT or an endpoint, outbound connections fail.

questions.prompt: What happens to an EBS root volume by default when you terminate an instance?
options: It is detached and stored free
questions.explanation: The root volume is normally set to delete on termination, which is why data must live elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is an EBS snapshot?
options: A running copy of an instance
A point in time backup of a volume
questions.explanation: Snapshots capture the volume contents at a moment so you can restore or clone it later.

questions.prompt: What is a custom AMI useful for?
options: Launching new instances that already have your configuration
questions.explanation: Baking configuration into an image makes new instances consistent and fast to start.

questions.prompt: When does an Elastic IP typically start costing money?
options: When it is allocated but not attached to a running instance
questions.explanation: AWS charges for reserved addresses that are sitting idle, to discourage hoarding.

questions.prompt: Why is object storage not the same as a filesystem?
options: Objects are stored whole with keys, not as files in directories
questions.explanation: S3 has flat keys that look like paths, but there are no real directories and no partial in place edits.

questions.prompt: What does aws s3 sync do on a second run?
questions.explanation: Sync compares source and destination and transfers only the differences.

questions.prompt: What does S3 versioning let you do?
options: Recover a previous version of an overwritten object
questions.explanation: With versioning on, overwrites and deletes keep the earlier version available for recovery.

questions.prompt: Why is Block Public Access on by default?
options: Because accidental public buckets are a common cause of data leaks
questions.explanation: Publicly readable buckets have caused many real world breaches, so the default is closed.

questions.prompt: What is a presigned URL used for?
options: Time limited access to a private object
questions.explanation: It grants temporary access to one object without making the bucket public.

questions.prompt: Which resource can quietly keep costing money after you delete an instance?
questions.explanation: Storage resources persist independently of instances and keep billing until deleted.

questions.prompt: What does S3 static website hosting not give you on its own?
questions.explanation: HTTPS on your own domain needs CloudFront in front of the bucket.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to let an EC2 instance read one S3 bucket?
options: Attach a role with a policy scoped to that bucket
Store root keys on the instance
questions.explanation: A scoped role gives exactly the access needed and nothing more.

questions.prompt: Snapshots are free to keep as long as you do not restore them.
questions.explanation: Snapshot storage is billed, which is why old ones should be cleaned up.

questions.prompt: Tagging resources with a project and owner makes cleanup and cost tracking much easier.
questions.explanation: Tags are how you find what belongs to what once you have more than a handful of resources.

questions.prompt: A bucket policy can lock you out of your own bucket.
questions.explanation: An overly broad deny can block even the account owner, which is why policies should be tested carefully.

questions.prompt: Why should a database sit in a private subnet?
options: So it cannot be reached from the internet
questions.explanation: A database with no public route removes the entire class of direct internet attacks.

questions.prompt: What is a DB subnet group?
options: The set of subnets RDS can place the database in
questions.explanation: RDS needs to know which subnets it may use, normally private ones across two zones.

questions.prompt: How should an application reach a private RDS instance?
options: From an instance whose security group is allowed on the database port
questions.explanation: Security group referencing keeps the path tight and avoids hardcoded IP ranges.

questions.prompt: What does RPO measure?
options: How much data you can afford to lose
questions.explanation: Recovery point objective is about acceptable data loss, measured in time since the last good backup.

questions.prompt: What does RTO measure?
options: How much data you can lose
How long you can afford to be down
questions.explanation: Recovery time objective is the target for how quickly service must be restored.

questions.prompt: What does a load balancer health check do?
options: Removes unhealthy targets from receiving traffic
questions.explanation: Failing targets stop receiving requests, which is what keeps the site up when one instance dies.

questions.prompt: What is a target group?
options: The set of instances a load balancer sends traffic to
questions.explanation: The target group holds the registered targets and the health check settings for them.

questions.prompt: What is ACM used for?
questions.explanation: AWS Certificate Manager issues and renews certificates for use with load balancers and CloudFront.

questions.prompt: Where does TLS normally terminate in a load balanced setup?
questions.explanation: Terminating at the load balancer means one certificate to manage instead of one per instance.

questions.prompt: Which metric is not collected by CloudWatch by default on EC2?
questions.explanation: Memory is inside the operating system, so it needs the CloudWatch agent installed to be reported.

questions.prompt: Why set a retention period on log groups?
options: Because storing logs forever costs money
questions.explanation: Log storage is billed, so indefinite retention quietly becomes a real cost.

questions.prompt: What is alarm fatigue?
options: So many alerts that people stop reacting to them
questions.explanation: Too many low value alerts train people to ignore the ones that matter.

questions.prompt: You should be able to reach your private RDS instance directly from your laptop.
questions.explanation: If you can, it is exposed, and the whole point of a private subnet has been lost.

questions.prompt: Moving application instances into private subnets behind a load balancer reduces their exposure.
questions.explanation: Only the load balancer is reachable from outside, so the instances have no direct attack surface.

questions.prompt: An automated backup is only proven once you have successfully restored from it.
questions.explanation: Untested backups fail exactly when you need them, so restoring is part of the process.

questions.prompt: Your site returns 502 through the load balancer. What do you check first?
options: Target health and whether the app is running
questions.explanation: A 502 means the balancer could not get a usable response, so the targets are the first place to look.

questions.prompt: The load balancer shows all targets unhealthy but the app runs fine over SSH. What is likely?
options: The instance type is too small
The security group blocks the health check port
questions.explanation: If the balancer cannot reach the health check path, targets are marked unhealthy even when the app works.

questions.prompt: An instance in a private subnet cannot download packages. What is the most likely cause?
options: No NAT gateway or a missing route to it
The AMI is out of date
questions.explanation: Outbound internet from a private subnet depends on a NAT route being present.

questions.prompt: You deleted the NAT gateway to save cost and now deployments fail. Why?
options: Private instances can no longer reach the internet
questions.explanation: Removing NAT removes outbound access, which breaks anything that pulls from the internet.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order when building the capstone architecture?
options: Network, then security groups, then instances
questions.explanation: The network and its security boundaries have to exist before anything can be placed inside them.

questions.prompt: Why give the load balancer, application and database separate security groups?
options: So each tier only accepts traffic from the tier above it
questions.explanation: Chained security groups enforce the tiers and stop the database being reachable from anywhere else.

questions.prompt: How do you prove an application instance is genuinely private?
options: It has no public IP and cannot be reached directly from outside
It is in a different region
questions.explanation: No public address and no inbound path from the internet is what private actually means.

questions.prompt: Which log would you use to trace one request from the edge into the application?
options: The load balancer access log and the application log together
questions.explanation: Matching the request across both logs shows exactly where it went and where it failed.

questions.prompt: What belongs in an incident write up?
options: What broke, how it was found, how long it took and what to automate
questions.explanation: The value is in the diagnosis and the follow up actions, not just the final command that fixed it.

questions.prompt: What is the point of a teardown checklist?
options: To make sure nothing keeps billing after you finish
questions.explanation: Forgotten resources are the main source of unexpected charges, and a checklist catches them.

questions.prompt: Which of these keeps billing after instances are terminated?
options: Unattached volumes, Elastic IPs and snapshots
questions.explanation: Storage and reserved addresses are billed independently of any running instance.

questions.prompt: Why draw the architecture before building it?
options: It exposes gaps and ordering problems before they cost you time
questions.explanation: A diagram forces you to decide what talks to what, which is much cheaper on paper than in the console.

questions.prompt: Knowing the daily cost of the stack you are running is part of doing this job properly.
questions.explanation: Cost is an operational metric, and engineers who cannot answer what it costs get caught out.

questions.prompt: If you can reach the application instances directly from the internet, the design is working as intended.
questions.explanation: Only the load balancer should be reachable, so direct access means the private layer has been broken.

questions.prompt: A written architecture diagram and incident report are worth more in an interview than a list of services you have used.
questions.explanation: They show judgement and operational thinking, which is exactly what a list of service names cannot demonstrate.
